displayQuote: I have never let my schooling interfere with my education

meta.title: Who really said "I have never let my schooling interfere with my education"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mark Twain. Grant Allen published the maxim in Post-Prandial Philosophy (1894); the first Twain credit found dates to a 1907 advertisement.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I have never let my schooling interfere with my education'?
meta.ogDescription: Grant Allen wrote it in 1894. Twain got the credit from 1907 onward — and the famous first-person wording is in neither man's work.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — actually Grant Allen
answer.sourceLine: The joke belongs to Grant Allen, who ended his essay “Eye versus Ear” in Post-Prandial Philosophy (Chatto & Windus, 1894) with: “What a misfortune it is that we should thus be compelled to let our boys’ schooling interfere with their education!” Allen liked it enough to reuse it in later novels. The familiar first-person wording — “I have never let my schooling interfere with my education” — appears in none of Mark Twain’s books, letters or speeches; the earliest Twain credit Quote Investigator located is a 1907 magazine advertisement.

source.heading: The 1894 essay that actually contains the joke

docMeta.dd: London: Chatto & Windus, 1894 (essays first ran in The Westminster Gazette)

source.excerpt:
One year in Italy with their eyes open would be worth more than three at Oxford; and six months in the fields with a platyscopic lens would teach them strange things about the world around them that all the long terms at Harrow and Winchester have failed to discover to them. But that would involve some trouble to the teacher.

What a misfortune it is that we should thus be compelled to let our boys’ schooling interfere with their education!
trail: 1894 — Grant Allen closes essay XV of Post-Prandial Philosophy with the maxim; the full text is at Project Gutenberg ↗.
1895 — Allen reuses it in The Woman Who Did, chapter I: “You wouldn’t let your schooling interfere with your education,” as recorded on Wikiquote ↗.
1907 — the first Twain credit located by Quote Investigator ↗: an advertisement in The Outing Magazine Advertiser, vol. 50, p. 840.
Today — the Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗ files the line under the apocryphal Twain and notes its post-2007 explosion on social media.

author.name: Grant Allen
author.kicker: The man who actually made the joke
author.heading: Grant Allen, the borrowed wit
author.bio: Grant Allen was born on Wolfe Island near Kingston in 1848, studied at Merton College, Oxford, and became one of the late-Victorian era’s busiest popularisers of evolution — roughly thirty novels between 1884 and 1899 alongside a steady stream of science essays. His scandalous bestseller The Woman Who Did (1895) made him notorious; his weekly Westminster Gazette columns, collected as Post-Prandial Philosophy in 1894, made him quotable. He died at Hindhead in 1899, and within a decade his best line had quietly changed owners.

misattribution.heading: How Twain ended up with Grant Allen’s joke
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of quote drift: a Victorian essayist’s aside, restated by him several times, then handed to the most quotable American alive and rewritten in the first person.

items.why: The line is absent from Twain’s books, letters and speeches. The Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗ lists it among the apocryphal Twain and notes that Twain in fact warned against people who bragged of lacking formal education.

Quote Investigator ↗ reports that the first instance it located crediting Twain appeared in The Outing Magazine Advertiser, vol. 50, p. 840 (1907), reading “Mark Twain once said: ‘Don’t let your boy’s schooling interfere with his education.’”

The boastful first-person “I have never let my schooling interfere with my education” matches none of the documented texts — Allen’s 1894 essay is about “our boys’ schooling,” and the 1895 novel variant ↗ is second-person.

misattribution.truthLine: Credit Grant Allen, 1894 — the wording is his, the fame is Twain’s, and the “I” is somebody else’s entirely. See Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.

context.heading: A joke about schools, told by a man with an Oxford degree
lead: Allen’s essay is not a shrug at learning — it is an argument that Victorian schooling taught words instead of things. “One year in Italy with their eyes open would be worth more than three at Oxford,” he wrote, before landing the line about boys’ schooling interfering with their education. The joke was the punchline of a case, not a slogan against study.

There is an irony the Center for Mark Twain Studies enjoys pointing out: Allen held an Oxford degree and began his career as a professor. And Twain, the man now credited with the quip, actually warned against people who bragged of having no formal education.
detailsBody: Allen’s 1894 form is third-person and about schoolboys: “let our boys’ schooling interfere with their education.” Wikiquote’s sourced Grant Allen page records a second-person version in The Woman Who Did (1895), chapter I: “You wouldn’t let your schooling interfere with your education.”

The 1907 advertisement that Quote Investigator identifies as the first Twain credit still keeps the third person: “Don’t let your boy’s schooling interfere with his education.” The boastful first-person “I have never let…” that circulates today is a later reshaping, documented in no work by either man.
context.pull: The way to learn every subject on earth, even book-lore included, is not out of books alone, but by actual observation.
